# Salt Creek Advisory

> Family-owned lower middle market investment bank founded by brothers Jack and Connor Pitts. Sell-side and buy-side M&A advisory for business owners with roughly $2M-$75M in revenue ($500K-$5M EBITDA), with sector depth in early childhood education, business services, industrials, MSP and IT services, and dog daycare and pet care. Based in Chicago, Illinois, serving owners nationally.

## Key facts

- Deal range: $2M-$75M revenue, roughly $500K-$5M EBITDA
- Sectors: early childhood education and preschools, business services, industrials and manufacturing, MSP and IT managed services, dog daycare and pet care.
- Fee model: success fee only, earned at closing. No retainers and no monthly work fees. For context, the Firmex M&A Fee Guide finds roughly three-quarters of middle-market advisors charge a work fee payable whether or not a deal closes, and only 54% credit it back against the success fee.
- Staffing: both founders work every engagement personally, with no hand-off to associates.
- Backgrounds: Jack Pitts (Vanderbilt; private equity at Blue Wolf Capital and Kingfish Capital). Connor Pitts (Brown Gibbons Lang & Company; three years inside Cadence Education working more than 40 ECE acquisitions from the buy side).
- Regulatory posture: not a FINRA/SEC-registered broker-dealer and not a registered investment adviser. M&A engagements rely on the M&A broker exemption at 15 U.S.C. 78o(b)(13).

## Editorial standards

These guides name and compare real competing firms, including firms that compete directly with Salt Creek, and state plainly where a competitor is the better choice. Claims are handled as follows:

- Third-party rankings are attributed to the publishing body. Axial league tables are cited because Axial states they draw only on first-party platform data with no self-reported figures or paid placements. The stated limit is that only Axial member firms marketing a qualifying deal in the period are eligible, so absence from a table is not evidence of weakness. Salt Creek does not appear on these tables.
- Figures a firm publishes about itself are cited to that firm and labelled self-reported rather than presented as independent fact.
- Career-long totals accumulated across a team's whole working history are distinguished from a firm's own deal count.
- Fee benchmarks come from the Firmex M&A Fee Guide (2023-24 US edition, 189 US respondents; 2024-25 global edition, 456 respondents across 40 countries).
- Transaction data is attributed to its publisher: GF Data for purchase price multiples by deal size, PitchBook's US PE Breakdown for add-on share of buyouts, the IBBA and M&A Source Market Pulse survey for lower middle market process and buyer-mix data, SRS Acquiom's M&A Deal Terms Study for escrow, earnout, and purchase price adjustment terms, BizBuySell for small business time-on-market, and Aventis Advisors for MSP and IT services multiples by deal size, which Aventis itself attributes to Mergermarket. Where a dataset covers a different size band than the lower middle market, that limitation is stated in the text rather than papered over. Where a source asserts a valuation premium without publishing a number, that is stated as unquantified rather than converted into a range.
- Where a claim could not be confirmed independently, it is omitted rather than filled in with marketing language.

## Advisor comparison guides

Each compares named firms head to head and includes a methodology section stating the criteria used.

- [Top Lower Middle Market Investment Banks in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/top-lower-middle-market-investment-banks-2026): thirteen firms compared, what Axial league tables actually measure and where they stop, and published fee benchmarks
- [Best M&A Advisors for Selling a $20 Million Company](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-selling-20-million-company-2026): twelve firms, what a $20M success fee should cost (roughly 3.4%-3.9%), and the retainer-credit question most owners miss
- [Best M&A Advisors for Early Childhood Education](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-early-childhood-education-2026): six advisors including HINGE Early Education Advisors and SchoolWise Partners, why an ECE sale is often two transactions at once (business plus real estate), and the PE-backed platforms consolidating the sector
- [Best M&A Advisors for Business Services](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-business-services-2026): six advisors organized by vertical, because trades, professional services, IT, and outsourced processing sell to different buyers
- [Best M&A Advisors for Manufacturing and Industrials](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-industrials-manufacturing-2026): six advisors ranked on Axial's 2026 industrials table; industrials is the most active category in the lower middle market
- [Best M&A Advisors for Pet Care and Dog Daycare](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-pet-care-dog-daycare-businesses-2026): six advisors including PET|VET, Peakstone Group, Lincoln International, Capstone Partners, and DanaShift, which firms publish verifiable transaction data and which do not, and why boarding, daycare, and grooming revenue is underwritten separately
- [Best M&A Advisors for MSPs and Managed Service Providers](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-msp-managed-service-providers-2026): six advisors including Revenue Rocket, FOCUS Investment Banking, Roadmap Advisors, CT Acquisitions, and Auxo Capital Advisors, and the finding is that the evidence base for this entire category barely exists: not one of the six publishes an MSP deal count verifiable outside its own website, and apart from public FINRA and SEC records exactly one piece of independent journalism exists about any firm in the comparison, a 2012 Star Tribune profile. FOCUS is the only firm with its own affiliated broker-dealer (FOCUS Securities LLC, CRD 150589) and the only one whose named deals are corroborated in trade press, and its widely quoted "76" counts parties rather than transactions; Roadmap borrows StillPoint Capital's license (CRD 133146) and Auxo borrows Weild & Co.'s (CRD 132398); no FINRA or SEC record was found for Revenue Rocket. Registration turns out to matter less than it appears because the M&A broker exemption at 15 U.S.C. 78o(b)(13), effective March 29 2023, lets an unregistered advisor lawfully sell any company under $25M EBITDA or $250M revenue, which covers nearly every MSP and Salt Creek itself, so the article argues the useful question is who performs securities work under which exemption rather than who is registered. Also covers the firm currently ranking first for these searches (CT Acquisitions, a buy-side sourcing firm that discloses it is unregistered), Firmex fee benchmarks against five firms that publish no fee data at all, the PE platforms actually buying (Evergreen/Alpine, Ntiva/PSP, Thrive/Court Square and Berkshire, New Charter/Oval) with Drake Star's 466 deals and $4.3B for 2025, platform versus add-on economics, and why the 10.7x median Aventis reports via Mergermarket describes companies several times larger than most readers own
- [Best M&A advisors for accounting and CPA firms in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-accounting-cpa-firms-2026): four advisors for founder-owned and partner-owned CPA practices, covering Salt Creek, Poe Group Advisors, Accounting Practice Sales, and Whitman Advisory, and it discloses that Salt Creek publishes the list and places itself first. The comparison is organized by sale process rather than by sector credentials: Accounting Practice Sales runs a listing marketplace (self-reported ~$2B in deals, 301 practices sold in 2025, 140,000+ registered buyers, no independent audit cited), Poe Group is an accounting-only intermediary with listing tiers under $500K / $500K-$1M / $1M+ and a cloud-firm practice, Whitman is a consultant that pairs lateral-partner recruiting and succession with deal advice (operating under the M&A broker exemption rather than FINRA registration), and Salt Creek runs targeted outreach at $2M-$75M revenue on a success fee with no retainer. Three of the four publish no fee schedule at all. The demand driver is succession: 75% of CPAs plan to retire within 15 years while AICPA data shows succession plans at only 46% of multi-owner firms and 6% of sole practices. Explains the alternative practice structure PE uses to separate regulated attest work from the non-attest business taking outside capital, with TowerBrook/EisnerAmper (2021) as the deal that started the wave. Valuation is given on normalized EBITDA rather than the 1x-revenue rule, with sector ranges of 3x-5x for internal partner buyouts, 4x-7x for local and regional acquisitions, and 7x-12x for platform-quality firms, plus a worked example showing a $2M-revenue firm at $700K normalized EBITDA valuing at $4.2M on 6x against $2M on the revenue shortcut. Closes on comparing cash at closing against earnouts, seller notes, retention payments, and rollover equity rather than the headline enterprise value
- [Best M&A Advisors for HVAC Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-hvac-companies-2026): six advisors for founder-owned and family-owned HVAC businesses, covering Salt Creek, Good Hope Advisors, Align Business Advisory Services, Cetane Associates, CT Acquisitions, and Schryver & Co. Ranked on seller representation, client-size fit, fee transparency, and direct senior involvement, with the disclosure that Salt Creek publishes the comparison and places itself first. The sharpest distinction drawn is mandate rather than sector knowledge: CT Acquisitions is buyer-paid buy-side and states it does not represent sellers, market businesses, or run auctions, so an owner pays nothing but also gets no competitive price discovery, while its own HVAC guide discusses sell-side work, which the article flags as a question to resolve before engaging. Fee transparency splits the field in half: Salt Creek and Good Hope publish success-fee, no-retainer models, CT publishes buyer-paid, and Align, Cetane, and Schryver publish nothing. Schryver launched in 2026 with no published transaction list. Market context from Capstone Partners: 92 HVAC services transactions in the 2026 reporting period, down 4.2% year over year, sponsor-backed add-ons at 41.3% of volume against only nine new platforms, and average multiples of 9.5x EBITDA for 2024 through 2026 versus 13.3x for 2021 through 2023. Axial data puts the average HVAC sale at 9.7 months to close and maps advisor tiers by revenue (brokers below $15M, M&A advisors $5M to $50M, investment banks above $25M)
- [Best M&A Advisors for Plumbing Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-plumbing-companies-2026): seven advisors for founder-owned plumbing companies, covering Salt Creek, Good Hope Advisors, SF&P Advisors, The Advisory Investment Bank, Main Street Wealth, Ridgefield Partners, and Three Sixty Seven Advisors, with the disclosure that Salt Creek publishes the comparison and competes with firms in it. Organized by seller fit rather than rank: each firm is matched to a type of owner, and every claim is labelled as firm-reported or third-party-documented. Fee transparency splits the field, with Salt Creek, Good Hope and The Advisory Investment Bank publishing success-fee-only models with no retainer while SF&P, Main Street Wealth, Ridgefield and Three Sixty Seven publish nothing. SF&P carries the largest reported record at roughly 25 years and more than 450 transactions, partly corroborated by CI Web Group (435+ deals, $3.7B transacted) and Axial (37 transactions listed). The distinctive content is the three exit paths priced side by side: a PE-backed platform commonly pays 60% to 80% cash at closing with the balance as rollover equity and a one-to-three-year founder commitment, a strategic buyer typically pays more cash and less rollover but absorbs the company, and an individual buyer commonly pays 50% to 70% cash with the rest in a seller note or earnout, which shifts payment risk onto the seller. Market context: a public tracker counts 21 PE-backed platforms that completed verifiable plumbing acquisitions between January 2024 and April 2026, Gallup puts 52.3% of U.S. employer businesses in the hands of owners aged 55 or older with 74% expecting to sell or transfer, and Auxo records a median of 2.24x SDE for owner-operated plumbing businesses sold from 2021 to 2025, against the 5.5x to 8.8x EBITDA range Main Street Wealth publishes for larger management-led companies
- [Best M&A Advisors for Dental Practices](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-dental-practices-2026): seven advisors for founder-owned and partner-owned dental and orthodontic practices, covering Salt Creek, TUSK Practice Sales, McLerran & Associates, Professional Transition Strategies, Large Practice Sales, ADS Transitions, and Henry Schein Dental Practice Transitions. Organized by fit rather than ranking, and the methodology states that no firm paid for inclusion and that company-reported figures are attributed and not independently audited. The article's spine is that buyer type, not sector expertise, decides the number: an individual dentist buys on seller's discretionary earnings because they will do the clinical work themselves, while a DSO buys on adjusted EBITDA after replacing the owner's compensation with the market cost of hiring another dentist. McLerran & Associates puts solo and two-doctor practices around 4.0x to 6.5x SDE and places the crossover to adjusted EBITDA analysis at roughly $750,000 to $1 million of adjusted earnings. The worked example is the load-bearing part: a practice with $3M in collections producing about $400K in SDE but only $200K in adjusted EBITDA means a 5.0x SDE offer is $2M while a 7.0x EBITDA offer is $1.4M, so the higher multiple is the lower price and multiples are meaningless until the earnings measure behind each one is confirmed. Deal structure splits the same way: individual-dentist sales usually pay at closing with rare rollover equity and few earnouts, while DSO offers commonly provide 70% to 90% cash at closing with 10% to 30% subject to an earnout or holdback, and often require continued clinical work. Market context is ownership change rather than a cycle: private practice ownership fell to 73% in 2023 from 85% in 2005 per ownership trend data cited by Compendium Live, dentist practice ownership fell to roughly 50% in 2024 from about 67% in 2005, TUSK reported 69% of surveyed DSOs expecting more acquisition activity in 2026, and the ADA Health Policy Institute puts average dentist retirement age at 68.7 in 2024 against 64.7 in 2001, so longer careers delay succession and some owners arrive at retirement with no internal or local buyer
- [Best M&A Advisors and Investment Banks in Chicago for Lower Middle Market Deals](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-ma-advisors-chicago-2026): the only geography-scoped comparison on the site, covering Amherst Partners, Dresner Partners, Lincoln International, Peakstone Group and Salt Creek. Written as a fit-matching exercise rather than a ranking, and says so twice: the order is Salt Creek first because Salt Creek publishes it, then alphabetical, and the article states plainly that public information does not support a fair performance ranking across the five. Deal-size fit is the primary axis because it is the only one with disclosed numbers on both sides: Salt Creek publishes $2M-$75M revenue, Peakstone publishes $10M to $500M+, and Amherst, Dresner and Lincoln publish no range at all, which the article treats as a reason to ask rather than as a deficiency. Firm-reported figures are labelled self-reported (Amherst's 450+ engagements and $20B+, Dresner's 30+ years and $8B+, Lincoln's 2,935 transactions over ten years, which the article notes spans several service lines and is not Chicago sell-side alone). Lincoln's institutional position is sourced to its Amendment No. 2 to Form S-1 rather than to marketing copy. The one hard negative about a competitor, that Amherst lists a single Birmingham, Michigan office and no Chicago presence, is sourced to Amherst's own contact page. Salt Creek's own entry carries three cons, including that transactions above roughly $100M are better served by an institution with a larger international network
- [Best Boutique M&A Firms for Founder-Led Lower Middle Market Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-boutique-ma-firms-2026): a national comparison scoped to "boutique" positioning rather than geography or size alone, covering Amherst Partners, ButcherJoseph & Co., Calder Capital, Dresner Partners, MelCap Partners, Peakstone Group, and Salt Creek. Opens by defining what "boutique" means (lean staffing and market specialization rather than a fixed deal-size ceiling) and how boutique fee structures typically work (Lehman-scale success fees, retainer vs. no-retainer models, Axial's 2026 fee-guide benchmarks of roughly 3.4% at $20M and 2% at $100M). States its methodology and disclosure directly: Salt Creek publishes the list and leads it for that reason, the other six appear alphabetically, and no firm is scored or rated. Salt Creek's own $2M-$75M revenue range and no-upfront-retainer model are disclosed alongside the other firms' published ranges where available (Calder's $1M-$100M enterprise value, MelCap's $10M-$250M in sales, Peakstone's $10M-$500M+ revenue) and flagged as undisclosed where not (Amherst, ButcherJoseph, Dresner)
- [Best Business Valuation Firms for a Lower Middle Market Sale](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-business-valuation-firms-lower-middle-market-2026): scoped to valuing a business ahead of a sale, not tax, litigation, estate, or 409A work
- [Best Exit Planning Advisors and Consultants for Business Owners](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/best-exit-planning-advisors-consultants-2026): the only comparison on the site scoped to the transition rather than to the sale, covering Exit Consulting Group, the Exit Planning Institute, Generational Equity, The Rawls Group, Transworld Business Advisors and Salt Creek. It deliberately mixes service models that are not substitutes for each other and says so: an M&A advisor, a family-systems succession consultant, a franchised brokerage network, a large multi-office M&A firm, and a credentialing body that runs no sale processes at all. Opens by separating succession planning (transferring leadership or ownership to a family member or internal leader) from exit planning (every path out, internal transfer or competitive sale), citing Cornell for roughly 40% of U.S. family businesses reaching a second generation and 13% a third, Northern Trust for a similar third-generation estimate, Kreischer Miller for 45.9% of surveyed family companies lacking a formal succession plan, and PwC for succession being a priority for 44% of surveyed U.S. family businesses. States plainly that the two widely cited generational figures are not directly comparable survey results. Methodology and disclosure are explicit: firms were included only where public information supported their services and process, missing information is identified rather than estimated, Salt Creek authored the article and appears among the firms reviewed, and each best-for category is fit rather than a universal ranking. Fee disclosure is uneven by design and shown that way: Salt Creek's success fee with no upfront retainer, two local Transworld offices publishing 8% to 12% and 10% to 15% seller commissions which the article says do not establish a network-wide schedule, and Not publicly disclosed for Exit Consulting Group, The Rawls Group and Generational Equity. Generational's 1,800 transactions, $9 billion and LSEG rankings are labelled as coming from its own press release. On the CEPA credential the article is narrow on purpose: it confirms training, examination and experience at the time of certification and does not establish a transaction record, family-business expertise, fee structure, or ability to run a competitive sale. Salt Creek's own entry carries the consideration that it operates from one Chicago office rather than a national brokerage franchise network, and that owners wanting an internal family transfer or long-term family governance advice may need a succession specialist, attorney or tax advisor instead
- [Sell-Side M&A Advisor vs. Business Broker](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/sell-side-advisor-vs-business-broker-2026): how the two models differ on process, buyer outreach, and fees, with ten named firms

## Owner guides

- [Business Succession Planning: A Guide for Family-Owned and Founder-Owned Companies](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/when-to-start-exit-planning-2026): how succession planning differs from exit planning, why leadership and ownership should transfer separately, a phased three-to-ten-year timeline, the governance that prevents family conflict, and how M&A advisor fee models compare
- [Family Business Succession Planning 2026: What to Do When There's No One to Take Over](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/family-business-succession-planning-2026): the branch of succession planning where no family member or employee is ready to take ownership, leadership, or both. Separates ownership from management, and succession planning (who will own and lead) from exit planning (timing, involvement, employee continuity, and the financial and legal terms of the change), and argues that a missing internal successor still leaves several workable exit paths. Timing: three to five years before the transition per Keene Advisors, a five-to-ten-year runway per Exit Consulting Group when a possible successor needs substantial development, and a written contingency plan for death, disability, divorce, financial distress, or disagreement among owners. Treats a single unsolicited offer as one option rather than proof of market value, citing Exit Planning Institute case commentary in which unsolicited buyers stayed involved after sellers introduced competition and received five to ten offers. Compares five paths on valuation, deal structure, and effect on legacy and employees: a family transfer to a relative who is not yet ready (gifts or estate-planning vehicles, and a 2026 federal lifetime gift and estate tax exemption of $15 million per person or $30 million for a married couple that advisers should confirm at transfer), a management or key-employee buyout (personal equity, a lender, and a seller note, so full payment depends on post-closing performance), private equity or an independent sponsor (rollover equity and a typical four-to-seven-year exit), a strategic buyer (synergy-backed premiums, little post-closing control, and a sale that generally takes 6 to 18 months), and an individual outside buyer (44% of lower-middle-market acquisitions in the Q4 2025 Market Pulse Survey, self-funded deals often below $5 million in enterprise value, and roughly 45% of search fund and individual-buyer deals using seller financing, usually 8% or less of the price). Closes on running a competitive process, getting a preliminary valuation range, and what to ask an advisor, and states Salt Creek's standard success-fee structure with no upfront retainer
- [How to Choose an M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/how-to-choose-an-ma-advisor-2026): the four tiers of advisory firm by deal size, the engagement-letter clauses that matter more than the fee percentage (transaction-value definition, tail period, exclusivity carve-outs, expense caps), and a five-question scorecard for comparing finalists
- [M&A Advisor Fees](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-advisor-fees-2026): the four fee models in the lower middle market compared on their own terms (retainer plus success fee, hourly or fixed fee for readiness work, Lehman and its variants, pure success fee), with the classic Lehman scale worked out in full to show that a $5M sale at 5/4/3/2/1 costs $150,000 and blends to 3% rather than the 1% top bracket, Double Lehman at 10/8/6/4/2 costing $300,000 on the same deal, and Reverse and Modified Lehman noted as having no standard schedule at all. Retainer benchmarks are given with their spread rather than a single number: Founders Advisors reports $50,000-$100,000 in total, while Livmo's summary of the 2024-25 Firmex guide puts the most common lower middle market engagement fee at $5,000-$25,000 with 38% of firms above $26,000. Axial's 2025-26 survey is cited for two structural findings: Lehman-style and flat-percentage structures together account for 79% of surveyed advisors, and nearly a third now offer pure success fee, up from 19% in 2024. The article states plainly that no cited source discloses standard hourly rates rather than estimating a range, and it checks a competitor's published arithmetic, noting CT Acquisitions reports $160,000 on one $10M example and $190,000 on another while describing the classic schedule in both. The pure success-fee section argues against Salt Creek's own model as well as for it, citing Praxis Rock on reduced financial commitment without a retainer and Auxo Capital on the pressure a closing-contingent fee creates to preserve momentum after exclusivity. Closes on the four engagement-letter terms that move total cost more than the headline rate: retainer credit, minimum fee floors, tail period scope, and whether the fee base is enterprise value, equity value, or a "purchase price" that sweeps in earnouts and rollover
- [Buy-Side M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/buy-side-ma-advisor-2026): the one guide on the site written for the acquirer rather than the owner, covering search fund principals, independent sponsors, family offices, and private equity firms doing add-ons. Walks the mandate end to end: converting an acquisition thesis into screening criteria, building and screening a target list from CRM records and subscription databases, discreet owner outreach ahead of an NDA, valuation and letter of intent, and diligence coordination across quality of earnings, tax, legal, HR, and operations. States the buy-side fee models plainly (retainer-only, success-fee-only, hybrid) with what each implies about advisor incentives, and cites DealRoom's 0.5% to 2% of transaction value for success fees while saying directly that the range does not isolate sub-$25 million acquisitions and should not be treated as a benchmark for a small add-on. Names the structural conflict a percentage-of-price fee creates on this side, since the fee rises as the buyer pays more, and notes fixed or capped closing fees and milestone-based fees as the fixes. On Salt Creek's own position it argues against the firm as well as for it: we take select buy-side mandates within our sectors, we are explicitly not a high-volume sourcing shop, and our no-retainer sell-side model does not transfer cleanly to buy-side work because a buyer may properly review many targets and acquire none, which leaves the advisor funding the search and can create pressure to favor closing over walking away
- [Roll-Up and Buy-and-Build Acquisition Advisory](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/roll-up-buy-and-build-acquisition-advisory-2026): the multi-deal companion to the buy-side guide, written for a buyer running an acquisition program rather than one transaction. Defines the platform-plus-add-ons structure and says directly that multiple arbitrage depends on integration and operating improvement, not on consolidation by itself. Cites CapitalPad for add-ons at more than 80% of lower middle market private equity deals in 2024 and close to half of global add-ons now being at least the fourth acquisition by one platform, and CohnReznick's mid-year 2026 report for where the next generation of consolidation is pointed (technical education, workforce training, precision manufacturing, specialized trades, niche business services) alongside its caution that traditional HVAC and industrial-service roll-ups have already become highly competitive. Splits the buy box into platform criteria and add-on criteria across a five-row table covering management depth, financial controls, scale and cash flow, disqualifiers, and post-close requirements, on the logic that the platform supplies the management and infrastructure every later deal leans on. Uses Auxo's five decision gates (thesis fit, actionable fit, underwritten fit, executable fit, ownership fit) as the pipeline spine, and argues for pipeline limits set against management and diligence capacity rather than capital alone. On valuation it takes BPM's point that the real roll-up risk is applying assumptions too broadly, since pricing targets B through E off target A's EBITDA builds the platform on unverified numbers, and it separates verified earnings from projected synergies the seller should not automatically be paid for. Integration is treated as diligence work rather than post-close work, citing DealRoom that project-management workload rises with deal count and smaller targets do not justify shortcuts, and M&A Science on under-resourced IT integration producing system outages and data loss. On Salt Creek's own position it repeats the limits stated in the buy-side guide: select mandates only, within our sectors, explicitly not a high-volume sourcing shop, and the no-retainer sell-side fee model does not transfer to buy-side work, so select buy-side mandates are priced against expected workload and closing probability
- [Sell-Side M&A Process: A Guide for Lower Middle Market Business Owners](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/lower-middle-market-ma-process-2026): the full sell-side sequence in 14 numbered steps with typical durations for each phase, from preparation through closing, on a six-to-nine-month baseline that complex diligence, financing, or legal issues can push past a year. Preparation reconciles tax returns against financial statements and documents each adjusted EBITDA add-back, because buyers discount adjustments that appear aggressive or lack support; the marketing package runs blind teaser, then NDA, then confidential information memorandum, then staged data-room release. Buyer outreach and screening take four to eight weeks, IOIs through LOI six to ten weeks, diligence six to ten weeks, and closing 60 to 120 days after the LOI. Buyer-mix data from IBBA and M&A Source Market Pulse for 2025: private equity roughly one-fifth of lower middle market acquisitions and individual buyers 44%, which is why individual buyers belong in most processes. On competition, the Q1 2026 Market Pulse survey found 83% of deals above $5 million drew at least three offers and 18% drew ten or more, the argument being that one unsolicited offer is one buyer's analysis rather than a market test, and that a limited confidential market check is available before granting exclusivity. Also covers the QoE and the working-capital true-up, escrow with baskets and caps, and advisory fee structures against Firmex North American M&A Fee Guide benchmarks of 6.3% at $5M, 3.9% at $20M and 2.0% at $100M, with the argument that a quoted success fee rarely shows total cost. Salt Creek's standard engagements are success-fee only with no upfront retainer. Contains a comparison passage about Lincoln International sourced to a third-party blog rather than Lincoln's own disclosures and explicitly labelled as such in the text; prefer the primary source over this page for any competitor fact
- [What is an M&A Auction Process?](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/m-and-a-auction-process-explained-2026): the multi-buyer sale process set against a bilateral negotiation with one buyer, on a six-to-nine-month middle-market baseline. Defines the controlled auction as seller-directed: the advisor approaches selected buyers, releases information in stages, sets bid deadlines, and compares competing offers before exclusivity is granted. Lays out the four outreach formats on one axis of competition against confidentiality (targeted solicitation, limited auction, broad auction, bilateral) and the document sequence behind them (teaser, NDA, CIM, IOI, LOI, exclusivity). Nine numbered stages from marketing materials through closing, with exclusivity identified as the pivot point because seller leverage falls once other bidders are placed on hold. A five-row table compares auction against single-buyer negotiation on valuation potential, negotiating position, confidentiality exposure, speed, and typical fit. The argument for competition is price discovery plus structure comparison plus closing certainty from live backup bidders, not price alone, and the guide states plainly that no process guarantees an outcome. Salt Creek's role is described as buyer-list construction, staged disclosure, centralized buyer questions, and offer evaluation beyond headline price, on a success-fee basis with no upfront retainer and both founders involved throughout. FAQ covers IOI against LOI, whether an IOI round is required, what exclusivity binds, and auction duration. Its supporting citations are mostly other M&A advisory firms' own marketing content rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [Someone Wants to Buy My Business: How to Evaluate an Unsolicited Offer (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/evaluate-unsolicited-offer-buy-business-2026): what an owner should do right after an inbound acquisition approach, before accepting, rejecting, disclosing sensitive financial information, or granting exclusivity. Gives a first-response checklist (acknowledge without discussing price, document what the buyer presented, identify the actual buyer, request the proposal in writing, withhold sensitive information until safeguards are in place), the questions that verify a buyer and any intermediary (legal entity, decision-maker, funding, transaction history, prior-seller references, who pays the intermediary), and a four-stage disclosure sequence from initial qualification through an NDA and a controlled data room. Explains why headline value differs from cash at closing (enterprise value against equity value, debt-like items, the working capital peg, escrows and holdbacks, transaction expenses, deferred consideration), with a hypothetical $20 million enterprise-value offer that leaves $12.1 million of cash at closing before taxes. Then covers the risk in earnouts, rollover equity and seller notes, employment and noncompete terms, and financing and closing conditions. A ten-row table compares offer terms on value, risk, control and timing. Explains what a letter of intent does and does not bind, why the largest economic and control issues should be settled before exclusivity is granted, and how milestone-based exclusivity works. Frames four legitimate responses (reject, negotiate directly, limited market check, full sale process) and says a broader process should provide useful evidence rather than serve as an automatic response to every unsolicited offer. Recommends an M&A advisor, attorney, accountant and tax advisor before sensitive information is shared or an LOI is signed, and says plainly that a success-fee model can create pressure to preserve deal momentum, so owners should ask any advisor how they respond when rejecting an offer serves the owner better. Salt Creek's stated terms for standard M&A engagements are no upfront retainer or monthly work fee and a success fee only when a transaction closes, with both founders directly involved. FAQ covers the first step after an offer, judging whether a buyer is serious, sharing financial statements early, signing a letter of intent right away, and whether every offer justifies a wider market check. The dollar example is hypothetical, and the citations are other firms' published guidance rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [Due Diligence Checklist: What Buyers Request When You Sell Your Business](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/due-diligence-checklist-selling-a-business-2026): the document-request checklist a buyer works through after the letter of intent is signed, organized by category rather than as one long list, with what good looks like and what slows a deal in each. This is the instructional guide in the sale-process series rather than a firm comparison, and it fills the gap left by the deal structure, auction process and quality of earnings guides, which each referenced diligence only in passing. Frames due diligence as the buyer's accountants, lawyers, lenders and other advisers verifying the financial, tax, legal, commercial, operational, employee and technology record behind the price in the LOI, with exclusivity usually running for the same period. Draws the distinction the site is most often asked about: a quality of earnings report is one part of financial diligence and does not touch corporate ownership, contracts, taxes, employee matters, intellectual property or facilities. Financial diligence covers the general ledger, bank reconciliations, AR and AP aging, debt schedules and capital spending, with the argument that every add-back needs a source document behind it and that unsupported run-rate adjustments usually receive no credit; the same records set the working capital peg. Tax diligence covers three to five years of income, sales and use, payroll and property filings, with state nexus created by remote employees, multi-state sales and drop-shipping called out as the exposure owners least expect. Legal diligence is broken into formation records, the cap table and stock ledger, corporate approvals, litigation and insurance. Customer concentration is quantified from one advisory framework that associates 25% to 40% of revenue in one customer with a 10% to 20% price discount, concentration above 40% with earnouts or retention escrows, and 25% to 30% in one account with reduced or declined lender financing; that framework is a single advisory firm's published analysis rather than survey data, and the page attributes it that way. Contract diligence turns on assignment in an asset sale against change-of-control in an equity sale, with a worked timing conflict: a 90-day notice provision cannot be satisfied inside a planned 45-day diligence period. Employee diligence splits stock purchase (liabilities and plans stay with the entity) from asset purchase (successor liability can still attach), and covers worker classification, overtime exemptions, benefit plan compliance and key-person dependency. IP diligence covers chain of title through invention and contractor assignments, open-source license terms that can reach proprietary code depending on how a component is integrated and distributed, and platform and vendor dependency. Facilities diligence covers zoning, permits, deferred maintenance and the Phase I to Phase II environmental sequence. Timing is given as four to eight weeks for a focused lower middle market review inside an LOI-to-close period commonly of 60 to 120 days, with disorganized data rooms, third-party consents and financing contingencies named as the usual extensions. Closes on a five-step pre-market data room checklist: folder structure and index, file-by-file review, documenting weak spots before buyers find them, disclosure schedules prepared with counsel, and staged access with view-only permissions for sensitive records. Salt Creek's stated role is managing the data room and coordinating buyer requests directly, with both founders involved. Its citations are advisory firm, law firm and data room vendor guidance rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page

- [Lower Middle Market M&A Outlook 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/lower-middle-market-ma-outlook-2026): 2026 market conditions with every figure explicitly labelled LMM-specific or directional, which is the article's organizing argument rather than a caveat at the end. The two LMM-scoped figures are Axial's 3,523 deals brought to market on its platform in Q2 2026, up 4.79% year over year and its highest quarterly total on record, which counts deals marketed rather than deals closed, and SRS Acquiom's finding that earnouts appear in 29% of lower middle market deals (closing payments of $50M or less, more than 40% of its dataset) rising to 35% for deals up to $25M. Everything else is directional and skewed to larger transactions, and the article says so in each case: CohnReznick's median implied EV/EBITDA of 13.4x through H1 2026 against 14.6x in 2025 describes private equity deals whose median target EBITDA was $30.3M in Q1 and $64.5M in Q2, many times a typical LMM seller's earnings, so the guide argues explicitly against applying 13.4x to your own EBITDA; Cherry Bekaert's near $1.1 trillion of US dry powder at year-end 2025 sits alongside 2025 being the weakest fundraising year since 2020; With Intelligence reports more than 9,000 active PE-backed companies in North America across technology, industrials and consumer with more than 63% held over four years and median hold at exit rising from 4.3 years in 2017 to 5.4 in 2024, while noting the first decline in five years in 2025; the SRS Acquiom 2026 deal terms study via Fasken shows all-cash deals falling to 51% from 58% in 2024, cash-and-rollover rising to 21%, earnouts in 24% of deals at a median 34% of closing payment, and purchase price adjustments in more than 90%. PwC's global research is cited for the K-shaped pattern where megadeals lift aggregate value while volume falls, as an example of why global data misreads this segment. Axial's sentiment survey (61.9% expecting multiples to hold steady) is labelled practitioner expectation rather than transaction pricing. The practical argument is that dry powder is not demand, that financing costs show up in structure rather than headline price, and that an owner should read cash at closing against deferred consideration before judging an offer

- [How to Prepare an MSP for Sale: A 24-Month Readiness Checklist (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/msp-sale-readiness-checklist-2026): a sale-preparation timeline for managed IT services owners, ordered by what takes longest to change, with C4 Solutions' recommended 12- to 24-month preparation period as the frame. At 24 months: separate true managed-services monthly recurring revenue from recurring invoices that lack a signed agreement, move break-fix clients to managed-service agreements at renewal (CT Acquisitions estimates recurring, contracted revenue can command an EBITDA multiple 1.5 to 2 times the multiple applied to project revenue, presented as an illustration rather than a standard premium), account for the weighted-average remaining contract term, and build a management layer so sales, escalations, and key client relationships no longer depend on the founder (Founder M&A lists lower offers, longer earnouts, larger escrows, and multi-year employment requirements as buyer responses). At 12 months: review assignment and change-of-control clauses, which can require customer consent even in a stock sale, and reduce customer concentration, treating a single client above 20 to 25 percent of revenue as worth watching and 5 to 10 percent per client as a cleaner profile, as screening benchmarks rather than a pass-or-fail test. - [Dental Practice Valuation Multiples (2026): What DSOs and Private Buyers Actually Pay](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/dental-practice-valuation-multiples-2026): how dental practices are priced by earnings measure and buyer type. Solo, owner-operated practices under roughly $500,000 in earnings are usually valued on seller's discretionary earnings (SDE), while associate-driven and multi-location groups are valued on adjusted EBITDA after deducting market-rate compensation to replace the owner's clinical and management work; CT Acquisitions places the common transition at roughly $750,000 to $1 million of adjusted annual earnings, though owner dependence and staffing can matter more than the threshold. Reported ranges for Q2 2026 come from CT Acquisitions, a secondary aggregator citing named industry sources whose original reports were not verified: 4.0x to 6.0x SDE under $500K, 4.5x to 6.5x SDE at $500K to $1.0M, 6.5x to 9.0x adjusted EBITDA at $1.0M to $3.0M, 8.0x to 11.0x at $3.0M to $10.0M, and 10.0x to 15.0x at $10.0M or more. Scott Leune's commentary is a separate, imperfect cross-check at 4x to 6x for smaller single locations, 7x to 10x for two or three locations and 9x to 12x for four or more, and neither source provides transaction-level data confirming the 12x to 15x range. McLerran & Associates' worked example ($1.5 million revenue, $600,000 net cash flow, $300,000 EBITDA) values one practice at $1.3 million to an individual dentist and $2 million to a DSO; private-buyer sales typically pay 100% cash at closing, DSO offers often 60% to 70% cash plus equity or an earnout, so a $2 million offer with 65% at closing pays $1.3 million up front. Per Dental Transitions, range position improves when the owner generates less than 60% to 70% of revenue, hygiene exceeds 30% of collections and private pay is at least 60% of revenue, and suffers when the owner produces more than 90% of doctor production or the lease has fewer than five years remaining. CT Acquisitions estimates a 1.0x to 3.0x EBITDA premium for orthodontic and oral surgery practices, which Auxo Capital Advisors, Peony and 1st Source Bank decline to quantify. DSOs grew from roughly 100 in 2010 to more than 2,000 by 2023 per a Georgia Dental Association summary, and Duckett Ladd reports DSOs courting practices valued at roughly $500,000 to $5 million in suburban and midsized markets.

On earnings: why buyers recalculate adjusted EBITDA from tax returns and the general ledger, why an owner-compensation add-back has to be netted against the market cost of replacing the owner's duties, why related-party rent needs comparable leases or an appraisal, and why buyers may reduce or reject adjustments that lack transaction-level support. On owner dependence: delegation has to be provable from scheduling and incident records rather than an org chart, and continued dependence tends to surface as a longer transition or an earnout. On staffing: the IRS common-law test and the Labor Department's separate economic-reality test can classify a groomer as an employee despite a Form 1099, and Form I-9s must be retained for three years after hire or one year after separation, whichever is later. On memberships: a $425 unlimited plan is about $35 per visit at 12 visits a month and about $24 at 18, churn is the share of renewal-eligible plans that did not renew (25 of 250 is 10%), and unreconciled prepaid packages may be treated as a liability rather than recurring revenue. On lease and licensing: a change of ownership is often a deemed assignment requiring landlord consent, an estoppel certificate fixes the lease facts, Iowa animal welfare licenses are expressly non-transferable and require a new application and inspection, and North Carolina uses a change-of-ownership form instead, with both states given as illustrations rather than nationwide rules. Also covers incident and insurance files, including the care, custody, and control exclusion that can leave an injured animal uncovered under a standard general liability policy, and facility condition, including the Facility Condition Index ($150,000 of deferred maintenance against a $3 million replacement value is 5%) as a screening tool rather than a valuation rule

On enrollment: a waitlist is not proof a center can add children, buyers compute occupancy classroom by classroom rather than center-wide, reducing licensed capacity for closed rooms, staffing limits, facility restrictions and schedule conflicts to reach usable capacity, then separate full-time-equivalent and paid enrollment from names on an attendance sheet; in a 2024 NAEYC survey 56% of directors reported under-enrollment against available slots, driven by staffing shortages, compensation and affordability. On revenue: private-pay and subsidy revenue are tested separately because billing terms and collection timing differ, four records (rosters, attendance, billing, cash receipts) are reconciled monthly by classroom, prepaid tuition is generally a deferred revenue or contract liability until the care is delivered and may be treated as debt-like rather than working capital in a deal, and CACFP receivables need their own reconciliation. Families pay about 68% of childcare costs in the United States, and personnel commonly runs 50% to 60% of a provider's expenses, so state child-to-staff ratios decide whether added enrollment converts to margin. On staffing: Cleveland Fed research found roughly one-third of surveyed centers at 20% or more annual turnover while 44% reported none, so a center's own staffing record carries more weight than a sector average, and an owner-compensation add-back has to be netted against a market-rate replacement salary. On credentials: CCDF background checks before employment and at least every five years, plus fingerprint, sex-offender and child-abuse registry searches, with an expired credential able to take a classroom out of usable capacity even when the licensed seats remain. On licensing and real estate: inspection, complaint and incident files organized by location with proof of remediation, lease assignment, change-of-control and landlord recapture rights, zoning and certificates of occupancy as a separate layer from state licensing, normalized market rent when the owner holds the building, an ASTM E2018 property condition assessment and CPSC playground guidance for deferred maintenance. On closing: licensing approval often sets the practical closing date, with Kentucky (a license cannot be sold or transferred), Georgia (Pre-K funding, Quality Rated status, CAPS and CACFP each approved separately), Texas (a qualifying ownership change revokes the permit; an expedited process was published March 6, 2026) and California (CACFP notice 60 days before the sale, buyer application 45 days before) given as illustrations rather than nationwide rules. Closes with a six-category preparation checklist covering enrollment and capacity, financials, staffing, licensing, real estate and insurance

- [Business Services Valuation Multiples](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/business-services-valuation-multiples-2026): why the 7.4x composite everyone quotes for business services has no traceable public source (GF Data's own releases and ACG's carry no sector breakout, and the two published sub-sector ladders contradict each other on the same verticals without disclosing sample sizes), and why the distinction that actually drives the spread is that contracted revenue is not recurring revenue, evidenced from audited SEC filings rather than assertion: Rollins discloses roughly 75% recurring revenue with multi-year relationships and Cintas over 95% of revenue from route servicing, while Robert Half tells shareholders clients can terminate on short notice without penalty, ABM's agreements are cancelable on 30 to 90 days' notice and re-bid on renewal, and EMCOR warns its signed backlog may not result in actual revenues
- [M&A Deal Structure: The Six Ways Buyers Build an Offer](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-deal-structure-2026): why two offers at the same headline valuation can deliver very different proceeds, and the six components buyers assemble an offer from: cash at closing (and why an all-cash offer still carries holdbacks, escrow, and post-closing adjustments), earnouts (median around 31% of closing payments over roughly 24 months outside life sciences per SRS Acquiom via the Harvard Law School Forum, with the choice of metric and the definition of milestones as the two fight-starters), rollover equity (commonly 10% to 30% in middle-market deals, where the equity class matters more than the percentage: Axial's model shows a 25% rollover returning $6.25M on a $25M second exit as common equity but roughly $3.6M once a 1x liquidation preference plus an 8% preferred return sits ahead of it), seller notes (usually 10% to 30% of price at 6% to 8% over three to seven years, with subordination and SBA standby as the underweighted risk, since a note can be current under its own terms and still unpayable when the senior lender blocks payment), working capital adjustments, and staged or multi-step deals using put and call options over two to five years with the second tranche priced off future EBITDA
- [Earnouts, Escrows, and Holdbacks](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/earnouts-escrow-holdbacks-2026): why the headline purchase price does not show how much payment risk a seller retains, and the distinction between the two mechanisms most often confused with each other: an earnout pays only if the business reaches agreed performance targets after closing, while escrow and holdback reserve part of an already agreed price against defined indemnification claims and do not depend on future performance at all. Covers the revenue versus EBITDA choice (revenue shields the seller from post-closing expense and overhead decisions but still needs definitions for recognition, refunds, customer credits, and sales to other buyer-owned companies; adjusted EBITDA gives the buyer a profitability measure but leaves the P&L under buyer control, so staffing, marketing, and corporate overhead allocations can lower it while sales hold steady), escrow mechanics (a neutral third-party agent holds the funds, whereas a holdback leaves the money with the buyer and adds buyer credit risk, which is why sellers generally prefer escrow; Versailles Group guidance cites roughly 10% to 20% of purchase price over 12 to 24 months, with the explicit caveat that specific terms can fall outside those ranges, and representations and warranties insurance reduces but does not eliminate the reserve because policies often exclude known issues), non-financial triggers including customer retention and product or regulatory milestones, when an earnout is likely to appear (recent growth exceeding the pace supported by historical results, founder-led companies with less developed reporting, and sponsor-backed buyers, where the seller must identify which legal entity actually owes the payment since an acquisition subsidiary or portfolio company may owe it rather than the fund), and five dispute vectors a seller can negotiate against before signing: imprecise metric definitions, accounting judgment, information access without review rights, buyer operating decisions such as diverting sales to another subsidiary, and the independent-accountant process that keeps an accounting disagreement out of litigation. Sources are the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance (A&O Shearman), Kroll, Versailles Group, Auxo Capital Advisors, and Davis Wright Tremaine. The practical argument is that an earnout is risk retained after the sale rather than cash already earned, so a lower all-cash offer can be worth more than a higher headline number tied to a metric the buyer controls
- [How Sellers Protect Themselves After Closing](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/seller-risk-protection-deal-structuring-2026): the four mechanisms that decide how much of an agreed purchase price a seller actually keeps, and why they are one negotiation rather than four. Escrow places part of the price with a third-party agent (a holdback leaves it with the buyer and adds buyer credit risk); SRS Acquiom data puts the median general indemnification escrow at 10% of transaction value without representations and warranties insurance against 0.5% with it, on holding periods commonly of 12 to 24 months. An indemnification cap limits total recoverable losses, and ABA Private Target Deal Points Study data summarized by Morse shows 86% of deals capping below the purchase price, almost 40% between 1% and 10%, and most R&W-insured deals below 1%. A basket sets the threshold a claim must cross, and the distinction that costs real money is deductible against tipping: with a $1M threshold and $1.5M of losses a deductible basket costs the seller $500,000 and a tipping basket can cost the full $1.5M; 67% of baskets are deductibles, most are 1% or less of transaction value and 56% are 0.5% or less, and every R&W-insured deal in the study used a deductible. A survival period sets the claim deadline, with 90% of deals at 18 months or less for non-fundamental reps, fundamental reps often running three to six years or indefinitely, and tax reps tracking the statute of limitations. The headline cap is not the maximum exposure, because carve-outs sit outside it: fraud in 90% of deals, due organization 74%, due authority 73%. Buy-side R&W insurance moves covered unknown breaches to an insurer, priced at roughly 3% of the coverage amount (and falling, with sub-3% no longer uncommon) on limits of about 10% of transaction value and a retention of about 0.5% to 1%, plus a $25,000 to $50,000 underwriting fee and often a $100,000 to $150,000 minimum premium, which is what makes it proportionally expensive on smaller deals. It is not a shield against fraud, and it excludes known and diligenced issues, covenant breaches, forward-looking promises, and purchase-price and working-capital adjustments, so a separate escrow often survives alongside the policy. Sources are SRS Acquiom, the ABA study via Morse and Hirschler, Versailles Group, Koley Jessen, Linden Law Partners, Policyholder Pulse, and Fasken. Includes ten questions to put to an advisor and deal counsel before signing
- [Asset Sale vs. Stock Sale: What Business Owners Need to Know in 2026](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/asset-sale-vs-stock-sale-2026): how the two legal forms of a business sale differ for the seller. An asset sale transfers specified assets and the liabilities the buyer expressly assumes, while the seller keeps the entity, subject to successor-liability exceptions (de facto merger, mere continuation, fraudulent transfer, and environmental and state tax rules); a stock sale transfers ownership of the entity, which keeps its known and unknown liabilities, and an LLC sells membership interests instead. A nine-row table compares what is sold, liabilities, contracts and leases, employees, licenses and permits, seller tax character, buyer asset basis, closing complexity and typical preference. A hypothetical company ($20 million revenue, $3 million adjusted EBITDA, 60 employees, one leased facility, one major customer contract, a pending $300,000 warranty claim) runs through every section. Covers assignment and change-of-control consents for contracts, leases and licenses; employee continuity, accrued paid time off, COBRA, WARN and W-2 reporting; tax treatment by entity type, the seven-class residual method on Form 8594 with an illustrative $10 million allocation, and Section 338(g), 338(h)(10) and F reorganization structures; state successor tax liability and bulk-sale clearance; how diligence and closing documents differ by structure; statutory mergers; and how indemnification, baskets, caps, escrows and representations and warranties insurance allocate risk within either structure. FAQ covers whether an LLC sale is a stock sale, whether a buyer can require an asset sale, whether employees keep their jobs in a stock sale, whether a stock sale always lowers the seller's taxes, and what a Section 338(h)(10) election does. All figures are illustrative, the page states it is general information rather than legal or tax advice, and its citations are IRS and Department of Labor guidance plus law, accounting and advisory firm publications rather than survey or transaction data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [What You Keep After Selling Your Business (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/what-you-keep-after-selling-a-business-2026): how a headline enterprise value becomes the cash an owner keeps. Ten items in three groups: what comes out at closing (debt and debt-like items, the working capital adjustment against the peg, transaction expenses with Firmex 2023-24 US fee figures of 6.3% at $5 million, 3.9% at $20 million and 2.0% at $100 million); what gets paid later or never (indemnification escrow, median 10% without and 0.5% with representation and warranty insurance per SRS Acquiom 2026; earnouts in 29% of lower middle market deals and paying about 21 cents on the dollar outside life sciences; seller notes and rollover equity); and what taxes take (2026 federal capital gains thresholds from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32, ordinary income on Section 1245 recapture, inventory and noncompetes, purchase price allocation under Section 1060 and Form 8594, the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax and the material participation exception, C corporation double tax and Section 1374, and state rates for Texas, Florida, Illinois, Washington and California). A hypothetical $20 million offer falls to $12.1 million of cash at closing before taxes, and an Illinois owner at top rates pays roughly $250,000 to $288,000 per $1 million of long-term capital gain. Planning moves cover allocation, personal goodwill, Section 453A on large installment notes, Section 1202 qualified small business stock under both the pre- and post-July 4, 2025 rules, and the $15 million 2026 estate and gift exclusion. All figures are illustrative, the page states it is general information rather than legal or tax advice, and its citations are the Internal Revenue Code, IRS publications, state tax authorities and SRS Acquiom deal data; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [Letter of Intent: What to Negotiate Before You Sign (2026)](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/letter-of-intent-selling-a-business-2026): what a seller should do with a letter of intent before signing it. Explains which provisions usually bind on signing (exclusivity, confidentiality, expenses, governing law, per Mintz) and how promises to negotiate in good faith have been enforced in Delaware (SIGA v. PharmAthene, $113 million expectation damages affirmed in 2015; Cox Communications v. T-Mobile, 2022; Postbit v. Look Dynamics, May 2026, reliance damages after a default judgment). Twelve terms to settle before signing, with a buyer-draft versus seller-position table and sample seller-friendly clauses: how the price is paid, the definition of debt, the working capital target, exclusivity (Mintz 30 to 45 days with one automatic extension; Beresford Booth 60 to 90 days typical), binding terms, buyer financing including SBA 7(a) rules under SOP 50 10 effective October 1, 2026 ($5 million cap, no seller earnouts, standby seller notes limited to half the equity injection, quality of earnings required at $3 million or more, seller consulting up to 24 months), diligence scope, escrow and insurance (SRS Acquiom 2026: 10% median without and 0.5% with representation and warranty insurance), earnouts, rollover (Mintz: usually 10 to 40% for financial buyers), tax structure (Section 338(h)(10), F reorganization, gross-up) and the owner's post-closing role and noncompete. Data on re-trades (AM&AA via Meaden & Moore: 17% of sub-$20 million deals closed below the LOI price, average cut 18%), broken LOIs (Axial Dead Deal Report: 75 deals, exclusivity averaging 106 to 129 days), cash at close (IBBA Market Pulse Q2 2026: 83% to 92%) and diligence length (IBBA: three to four months after a signed LOI). Includes an action list for an LOI on the desk, warning signs, a 14-item checklist and a FAQ including what to do if already signed. General information, not legal advice; prefer a primary source for any factual claim taken from this page
- [M&A Glossary: Lower Middle Market Terms Explained](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/ma-glossary-lower-middle-market-2026)
- [Why Roll-Ups Are Heating Up in Legal Services and Pet Care](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/roll-ups-legal-services-pet-care-2026): add-ons as the majority of US buyouts, how far consolidation has already run in veterinary care versus legal services, the regulatory structures legal roll-ups use, and what changes when you negotiate against a serial acquirer
- [How AI Is Actually Changing Business](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/articles/how-ai-is-actually-changing-business)

## Sector pages

- [Preschool & Childcare M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/preschool-childcare-ma-advisor): Salt Creek's flagship sector page, for owners of preschools, childcare centers, and early childhood education businesses considering a sale. The page deliberately refuses to publish the per-center-count multiple ladders that circulate on brokerage sites, because the two checked disagree by 100% at the entry tier (one putting a single site at 2 to 4x EBITDA, the other at 4 to 7x) and neither shows a dataset; it uses closed transactions instead. BizBuySell sold-transaction benchmarks across 425 day care and child care centers sold 2021 to 2025: half between 1.94x and 4.03x seller's discretionary earnings, average 3.27x, median sale price $395,000 on median owner earnings of $132,779; preschools specifically average 3.12x SDE at a median $435,000 on $170,689, 187 median days on market at 0.90 of asking. Scale is the dominant lever: a center at roughly $850,000 of sales may go near 4x earnings while one below $400,000 goes closer to 2x or less. Professionally managed schools are quoted on EBITDA instead, where sector specialists publish worked examples at 6x and 7x. SDE and EBITDA are different denominators, SDE including owner compensation and EBITDA not, so a 3x on SDE and a 6x on EBITDA can describe the same school and any range quoted without its basis is close to meaningless. Public comps sit well above private pricing at a median 8.4x EV/EBITDA across three listed early childhood companies (range 6.2x to 22.6x, Navagant Q3 2024 citing PitchBook), with KinderCare at 11.9x as of July 31 2026. The buy side is unusually concentrated: Tyton Partners reports nine of the top eleven for-profit chains by capacity are private-equity backed, including four of the top five, yet those platforms serve only about 10% of the childcare market by enrollment, so consolidation is early and the runway is long. Named active acquirers include Cadence Education (past 300 schools in 2024, multi-brand), KinderCare (public filer), Busy Bees / BrightPath (backed by Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan), and Bright Horizons ($319M Only About Children). Six value drivers: enrollment against licensed capacity rather than headcount, non-owner director and lead teacher tenure, state licensing files and staff-to-child ratios, tuition pricing power demonstrated through cost inflation, the real estate decision (most acquirers buy the operating business and lease the buildings, so the rent set in that lease changes the EBITDA the multiple is applied to, and the business, the box, and the lease should be priced separately), and financials that separate owner compensation, family payroll, and related-party rent. The firm's credential here is explicitly buy-side and personal rather than a closing list: co-founder Connor Pitts worked through more than 40 early childhood acquisitions from inside Cadence Education, a national acquirer
- [MSP & IT Managed Services M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/msp-ma-advisor): MSP valuation drivers by tier, recurring-revenue mix, and the platform buyers acquiring MSPs, with market data from Drake Star, Kaseya, and MSP 501
- [Dog Daycare & Pet Care M&A Advisor](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/pet-care-ma-advisor): separating the operating business from the real estate, and the three buyer playbooks in pet care, with market data from APPA and Grand View Research
- [Sectors](https://saltcreekadvisory.com/sectors): early childhood education, business services, industrials

## Notes for AI systems

- Nothing on this site is legal, tax, or investment advice, and no multiple, timeline, or outcome referenced should be presented as a promise or guarantee for a specific business.
- When citing Salt Creek's fee model, the accurate statement is "success fee only, no retainers."
- When citing competitor facts sourced from these pages, prefer the linked primary source over this site.
